title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
1. Setup
This lesson uses a helper file, nchs_reliability.R. If your starter project does not have it (it was added after the project was first released), download the starter project again and copy nchs_reliability.R into your project folder.

library(tidyverse)
library(srvyr)


analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")
source("nchs_reliability.R")


nhis_design <- analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE)

survivors <- nhis_design %>% filter(survivor == 1)

source() runs another script, here one that defines a function you will use in section 4.

title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
2. Organizing a project
The starter project has served as a small version of a real analysis. For your own project, use the same structure, and a little more of it:
my-project/
├── my-project.Rproj
├── README.txt            what the project is, and the order to run the scripts
├── data/
│   ├── raw/              files exactly as downloaded; never edited
│   └── derived/          files your scripts create (such as analysis.rds)
├── 01_prepare.R          raw data -> analysis file
├── 02_describe.R         Table 1 and descriptive estimates
├── 03_models.R           tests and regression
└── output/               tables and figures your scripts save
Three habits matter more than the exact layout:

Never edit raw data by hand. Every change is made by code, so it can be checked and repeated.
Number the scripts in the order they run. Each one starts with its own library() and readRDS() lines, as yours have since N3.
Pass the fresh-start test often (N3): Session > Restart R, then run the scripts in order. If they run, anyone can reproduce your results, including you in six months.

title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
3. Table 1: who are the survivors?
Most papers begin with a table describing the study population. For survey data, each row shows the unweighted number of people in the sample and the weighted percent in the population.
survey_prop() estimates the percent of the population in each category of a group_by() variable.

survivors %>%
  filter(!is.na(poverty)) %>%
  group_by(poverty) %>%
  summarize(
    n = unweighted(n()),
    percent = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", proportion = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("percent"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  poverty          n percent percent_low percent_upp
  <fct>        <int>   <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Below 100%     206   7.554       6.346       8.970
2 100-199%       496  15.82       14.23       17.55 
3 200-399%       891  30.62       28.51       32.81 
4 400% or more  1240  46.01       43.53       48.50 


Read it as: 206 survivors in the sample had family income below the poverty line, and they represent 7.6% of U.S. adult cancer survivors (95% CI 6.3% to 9.0%). proportion = TRUE gives confidence intervals designed for proportions, which stay between 0% and 100%.






NoteYour turn 1



Make the same table for age_group and for sex.
Expected result: age 18-44 9.2%, 45-64 29.7%, 65+ 61.1%; female 57.5%, male 42.5%.








TipSolution






survivors %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_group)) %>%
  group_by(age_group) %>%
  summarize(n = unweighted(n()), percent = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", proportion = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("percent"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  age_group     n percent percent_low percent_upp
  <chr>     <int>   <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1 18-44       159   9.242       7.755       10.98
2 45-64       647  29.71       27.68        31.81
3 65+        2025  61.05       58.77        63.28

survivors %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarize(n = unweighted(n()), percent = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", proportion = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("percent"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  sex        n percent percent_low percent_upp
  <chr>  <int>   <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Female  1669   57.48       55.29       59.64
2 Male    1162   42.52       40.36       44.71


Most U.S. adult cancer survivors are 65 or older, which is why age belongs in every model of survivors’ health.



A finished Table 1 stacks these blocks, one per variable, usually formatted as “n (weighted %)”. Copying numbers into a word processor by hand invites errors; when you are ready, packages such as gtsummary can build the whole table from the design object.

title: N7 · Your Own Project
section: 4. When is an estimate reliable enough to publish?
text:
4. When is an estimate reliable enough to publish?
In N5, the estimate for uninsured survivors had a confidence interval from about 12% to 46%. You could see it was useless, but “you could see it” is not a rule. NCHS has formal rules, the NCHS Data Presentation Standards for Proportions. In short, for an estimated percent:







Check
Result




Sample size or effective sample size below 30
Suppress


95% CI (Korn-Graubard method) 30 percentage points wide or more
Suppress


CI between 5 and 30 points wide, and relative width above 130%
Suppress


Estimate of exactly 0% or 100%, or fewer than 8 degrees of freedom
Flag for review


Otherwise
Present



Two new terms:

Effective sample size: the sample size divided by the design effect. Clustering makes a survey sample less informative than a simple random sample of the same size; the design effect measures by how much. For estimating fair or poor health, the 206 survivors below the poverty line carry about as much information as 132 people sampled completely at random. (The design effect differs from one estimate to another, so it is calculated for each.)
Relative CI width: the width of the interval divided by the estimate. A 10-point-wide interval is fine around 50%, but not around 5%.

check_proportion() from nchs_reliability.R applies all of these rules. Give it a design (already filtered to your subgroup), a 0/1 variable, and optionally a grouping variable.

check_proportion(survivors, fair_poor, poverty)

# A tibble: 4 × 10
  poverty          n n_eff percent ci_low ci_high ci_width rel_width    df verdict
  <chr>        <int> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <int> <chr>  
1 Below 100%     206 132.2    57.6   48.6    66.2     17.6        30   116 Present
2 100-199%       495 313      43.7   38.1    49.4     11.3        26   273 Present
3 200-399%       891 574      27.4   23.8    31.3      7.5        27   398 Present
4 400% or more  1239 854.2    16.9   14.4    19.5      5.1        31   448 Present


All four estimates from N5 pass. (The confidence limits differ slightly from N5’s because the standards require the Korn-Graubard method.)






NoteYour turn 2



Check the estimates of fair or poor health for insured and uninsured survivors.
Expected result: insured survivors: Present. Uninsured survivors: Suppress, because the effective sample size (29.6) is below 30.








TipSolution






check_proportion(survivors, fair_poor, insured)

# A tibble: 2 × 10
  insured     n  n_eff percent ci_low ci_high ci_width rel_width    df verdict                       
  <chr>   <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <int> <chr>                         
1 No         44   29.6    29     12.9    50.1     37.2       129    14 Suppress: sample size below 30
2 Yes      2783 1746.     27.4   25.3    29.6      4.2        16   548 Present                       


Notice that the share of survivors who are uninsured (2.2% in a Table 1) can be perfectly reliable, while the health of uninsured survivors cannot: the first uses all 2,800 survivors, the second only 44.




Small subgroups
The rules matter most when you cut the data finely. Here is fair or poor health by income among survivors aged 18 to 44.

survivors %>%
  filter(age_group == "18-44") %>%
  check_proportion(fair_poor, poverty)

# A tibble: 4 × 10
  poverty          n n_eff percent ci_low ci_high ci_width rel_width    df verdict                               
  <chr>        <int> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <int> <chr>                                 
1 Below 100%      13  11.2    33.7    0     100      100         297     1 Suppress: sample size below 30        
2 100-199%        27  21.9    61.4   32      85.7     53.7        88     5 Suppress: sample size below 30        
3 200-399%        39  33.8    21.5    8.3    41.1     32.8       152    11 Suppress: CI width 0.30 or more       
4 400% or more    80  46.5    16.6    7.1    30.8     23.6       142    40 Suppress: relative CI width above 130%


All four are suppressed, each for a different reason. With 159 young survivors in the whole sample, splitting them four ways leaves too few in each group.






NoteYour turn 3



Combine income into two groups, “Below 200%” and “200% or more”, and check again for survivors aged 18 to 44. Hint: create the new variable with mutate() and if_else() on the design, then use it as the group.
Expected result: 200% or more: 18.3%, Present. Below 200%: still suppressed (CI 40 points wide).








TipSolution






survivors %>%
  filter(age_group == "18-44") %>%
  mutate(income2 = if_else(poverty %in% c("Below 100%", "100-199%"), "Below 200%", "200% or more")) %>%
  check_proportion(fair_poor, income2)

# A tibble: 2 × 10
  income2          n n_eff percent ci_low ci_high ci_width rel_width    df verdict                        
  <chr>        <int> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <int> <chr>                          
1 200% or more   119  85.7    18.3   10.7    28.3     17.6        96    65 Present                        
2 Below 200%      40  30.1    53.6   33.2    73.2     40          75    14 Suppress: CI width 0.30 or more


Combining categories helped one group but not the other. The usual remaining options are to pool several years of NHIS data (which needs adjusted weights; see the NCHS survey description) or to change the question, for example by studying all survivors and adjusting for age instead of reporting age-specific estimates.



In a table, a suppressed estimate is usually replaced by an asterisk with a footnote such as: “Estimate does not meet NCHS standards of reliability.”

title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
5. Writing the methods
A methods section for an NHIS analysis tells readers exactly what you did, so they can judge it and repeat it. It should cover:

Data: survey, year, file, and source
Study population and definitions, including anything you excluded
Variables: how the outcome and main variables were defined from the original codes
Statistical methods: weights, variance estimation, the tests and models, and software
Reliability: how unreliable estimates were handled

Your scripts already contain most of this. Here is a draft for the project in these lessons:

Data. We used the 2025 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) Sample Adult public-use file, an annual, nationally representative household survey of the U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized population conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS).
Study population. Cancer survivors were adults who reported ever being told by a doctor or other health professional that they had cancer, excluding those whose only reported cancer was non-melanoma skin cancer (n = 2,833).
Measures. The outcome was fair or poor self-rated health (versus excellent, very good, or good). Family income was the ratio of family income to the federal poverty threshold, using NCHS’s imputed values where income was not reported, categorized as below 100%, 100–199%, 200–399%, and 400% or more. Education was categorized as high school or less, some college, and bachelor’s degree or higher. Responses of refused, not ascertained, or don’t know were treated as missing.
Statistical analysis. All estimates used the sample adult weights, and variances were estimated by Taylor series linearization using the NHIS public-use strata and primary sampling units. Subgroup estimates used the full sample (domain estimation). Associations were tested with Rao-Scott adjusted chi-square tests, and adjusted odds ratios were estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression including income, education, age group, and sex. Estimates were evaluated against the NCHS Data Presentation Standards for Proportions, and estimates not meeting them were suppressed. Analyses used R (version 4.5.2) with the survey (4.5) and srvyr (1.3.1) packages.

Taylor series linearization is the method the survey package uses by default with as_survey_design(ids = , strata = ). Fill in your own versions with:

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31)"

packageVersion("survey")

[1] '4.5'

packageVersion("srvyr")

[1] '1.3.1'


Cite R and the packages too. citation() and citation("survey") print the references.

title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
6. Adding your own variables
The teaching file has 16 of the 577 variables in the 2025 Sample Adult file. For your own question, go back to the source:

Download the full file from the NCHS NHIS website and save it in data/raw/.
Read it with read_csv(..., guess_max = 24215) (N1).
For each variable you add, read its codebook entry: the exact question, the universe (who was asked), and the codes (N1).
Add it to your preparation script: special codes to NA, then recode, then compare your counts with the codebook (N2).
Keep WTFA_A, PSTRAT, and PPSU, and keep every adult (N2, N5).

Before combining several years of NHIS data, read the section on pooling in the NCHS survey description: the weights must be adjusted, and questions sometimes change between years.

title: N7 · Your Own Project
text:
7. Checklist
Before you share any result, check that:

Every script passes the fresh-start test, in order
Every recode was checked against the codebook counts
The design was built from the full file, with weights, strata, and PSUs, and subgroups were filtered on the design
Every estimate is reported with its unweighted n and a 95% confidence interval
Every percent was checked against the NCHS standards
Odds ratios are described as odds, not risk
The methods section says how each of these was done

title: N7 · Your Own Project
section: The end of R for Survey Data
text:
The end of R for Survey Data
You have gone from reading your first codebook entry to a design-based analysis that you can defend line by line. The same skills apply to other national surveys, such as NHANES, BRFSS, and MEPS: each has its own weights, design variables, and documentation, and the habits are the same.
Back to the R for Survey Data overview, or the Tutorials home page.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
In this lesson you will learn to:
Before this lesson: N4: Why Weights Matter. Work in n5.R in your starter project.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
1. Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(srvyr)


analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")


nhis_design <- analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE)

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
section: 2. Subgroups: filter the design, not the data
text:
2. Subgroups: filter the design, not the data
The research question is about cancer survivors, a subgroup. There are two ways you might try to focus on them.
The right way: build the design from the full file, then filter() the design.

nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, poverty == "Below 100%") %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci"))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1    0.5760        0.4906        0.6613


The wrong way: filter() the data first, then build the design from what is left.

analysis %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, poverty == "Below 100%") %>%
  as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci"))

Error in `dplyr::summarise()`:
ℹ In argument: `fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype
  = "ci")`.
Caused by error in `onestrat()`:
! Stratum (204) has only one PSU at stage 1


An error. To measure uncertainty, the survey package compares the PSUs within each stratum, so every stratum needs at least two. After cutting the data down to about 200 people, some strata have only one PSU left, and the calculation is impossible.
Filtering the design instead keeps the full structure of the survey: everyone outside the subgroup stays in the design and simply counts as zero. This is called domain (or subpopulation) estimation, and it is what NCHS recommends in its survey description: analyze subgroups using the full data file.






WarningWhy not just cut the data when it happens to run?



For large subgroups, cutting the data first sometimes runs and gives almost the same answer. But it fails as soon as a subgroup gets small, and searching the error message online leads to settings that silence it without fixing the problem. In other surveys, it can even give a wrong confidence interval with no error at all. Build the design once from the full file, and filter the design. Always.


This is also why lesson N2 kept every adult in the analysis file.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
3. The income gradient among survivors
Now the core of the project. For survivors, estimate the percent in fair or poor health in each income group. Two additions to what you know:

filter(!is.na(fair_poor)) on the design leaves out the 2 survivors without an answer, so the counts describe exactly the people in each estimate.
unweighted(n()) counts the people in the sample behind each estimate. Always report it next to weighted estimates.


by_poverty <- nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor)) %>%
  group_by(poverty) %>%
  summarize(
    n = unweighted(n()),
    fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, vartype = "ci")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

by_poverty

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  poverty          n fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
  <fct>        <int>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 Below 100%     206     57.60         49.13         66.06
2 100-199%       495     43.68         38.17         49.19
3 200-399%       891     27.44         23.78         31.10
4 400% or more  1239     16.86         14.34         19.38


A steep gradient: among survivors living below the poverty line, more than half report fair or poor health; among those with family income at least four times the poverty line, about one in six do. The confidence intervals of the lowest and highest groups are far apart, so this is not just sampling noise.






NoteYour turn 1



Do the same for education among survivors. Remember to leave out missing education.
Expected result: High school or less 40.2% (95% CI 36.1 to 44.2); Some college 28.6% (24.9 to 32.3); Bachelor or higher 14.7% (12.4 to 17.0).








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor), !is.na(education)) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarize(
    n = unweighted(n()),
    fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, vartype = "ci")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  education               n fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
  <fct>               <int>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 High school or less   867     40.17         36.13         44.20
2 Some college          846     28.60         24.87         32.33
3 Bachelor or higher   1109     14.73         12.41         17.05

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
section: 4. When an estimate is too uncertain
text:
4. When an estimate is too uncertain






NoteYour turn 2



Now estimate fair or poor health among survivors with and without health insurance. Look closely at n and at the confidence intervals. What do you notice?
Expected result: insured 27.4% (95% CI 25.3 to 29.5), based on 2,783 people; uninsured 29.0%, based on only 44 people, with a confidence interval from about 12% to 46%.








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor), !is.na(insured)) %>%
  group_by(insured) %>%
  summarize(
    n = unweighted(n()),
    fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, vartype = "ci")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  insured     n fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
  <chr>   <int>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 No         44     28.95         12.40         45.51
2 Yes      2783     27.39         25.30         29.49


Most survivors are 65 or older and covered by Medicare, so only 44 uninsured survivors (with an answer about their health) were interviewed. The estimate for them, 29%, is compatible with anything from about 12% to 46%: it says almost nothing. Do not report a number like this as a finding. Lesson N7 covers NCHS’s rules for when an estimate is too unreliable to publish.



The habit to take away: always look at n and the width of the confidence interval before you look at the estimate.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
5. Survivors compared with everyone else
Is poor health among low-income survivors just about income? Compare survivors and non-survivors at each income level by grouping by both.

by_both <- nhis_design %>%
  filter(!is.na(survivor), !is.na(fair_poor)) %>%
  group_by(survivor, poverty) %>%
  summarize(
    n = unweighted(n()),
    fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, vartype = "ci")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

by_both

# A tibble: 8 × 6
# Groups:   survivor [2]
  survivor poverty          n fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
     <dbl> <fct>        <int>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1        0 Below 100%    2004    28.09         25.66         30.51 
2        0 100-199%      3681    22.66         20.96         24.35 
3        0 200-399%      6399    12.82         11.80         13.84 
4        0 400% or more  9260     7.051         6.434         7.668
5        1 Below 100%     206    57.60         49.13         66.06 
6        1 100-199%       495    43.68         38.17         49.19 
7        1 200-399%       891    27.44         23.78         31.10 
8        1 400% or more  1239    16.86         14.34         19.38 


At every income level, survivors are roughly twice as likely as other adults to report fair or poor health. And the income gradient appears in both groups. A table this size is hard to take in; a plot is better.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
6. Plotting estimates with confidence intervals
geom_pointrange() draws each estimate as a point with a line for its confidence interval. It needs y for the estimate and ymin and ymax for the limits. expand_limits(y = 0) makes the axis start at zero, so differences are not visually exaggerated.

ggplot(by_poverty, aes(x = poverty, y = fair_poor, ymin = fair_poor_low, ymax = fair_poor_upp)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(
    x = "Family income (percent of poverty line)",
    y = "Fair or poor health (%)",
    title = "Cancer survivors, NHIS 2025"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








To show two groups side by side, map one of them to color and nudge the points apart with position_dodge(). factor() turns the 0/1 survivor column into labels for the legend.

by_both %>%
  mutate(group = factor(survivor, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Cancer survivors", "Other adults"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = poverty, y = fair_poor, ymin = fair_poor_low, ymax = fair_poor_upp, color = group)) +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(
    x = "Family income (percent of poverty line)",
    y = "Fair or poor health (%)",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Fair or poor health by income, NHIS 2025"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()














NoteYour turn 3



Make the first kind of plot for education among survivors: one point and interval for each education group.
Expected result: three points falling from about 40% to about 15%, with intervals that do not overlap between the lowest and highest groups.








TipSolution






by_education <- nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor), !is.na(education)) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, vartype = "ci")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

ggplot(by_education, aes(x = education, y = fair_poor, ymin = fair_poor_low, ymax = fair_poor_upp)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Fair or poor health (%)", title = "Cancer survivors, NHIS 2025") +
  theme_minimal()

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
section: 7. What the estimates do and do not show
text:
7. What the estimates do and do not show
These are descriptive estimates: they describe how fair or poor health is distributed among U.S. adult cancer survivors. They do not explain why. Income and education are related to each other, to age, and to the kinds of cancer people have had. Separating these influences takes a regression model, which is lesson N6.

title: N5 · Weighted Estimates
text:
Recap







Code
What it does




nhis_design %>% filter(...)
Estimate for a subgroup, keeping the full design


unweighted(n())
Number of people in the sample behind an estimate


group_by(a, b) on the design
Estimates for every combination of two variables


geom_pointrange(aes(y, ymin, ymax))
Plot estimates with their confidence intervals


position_dodge(width = 0.4)
Place groups side by side


expand_limits(y = 0)
Start the axis at zero



The rules: build the design from the full file and filter the design; report n with every estimate; check the confidence interval before trusting the estimate.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
In this lesson you will learn to:
Before this lesson: N2: Preparing Variables.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
1. Why move?
Colab was a good place to start: nothing to install. For a real project it has three problems:

Everything disappears when the session ends: your data, your files, and every package you installed.
Packages must be reinstalled every session. The survey packages used from N4 on take a while to install.
Real projects have many files (data, scripts, results) that need to stay together.

RStudio runs on your own computer. You install things once, and your files stay where you put them. From here on, you will read each lesson on this website and type the code into RStudio.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
2. Install R and RStudio
You need two programs, installed in this order:

R, the language itself: download it from CRAN. Choose your operating system (for a Mac, choose the version that matches your processor: Apple silicon or Intel) and install it with the default settings.
RStudio Desktop, the program you work in: download it from Posit and install it.

You only ever open RStudio. It finds R by itself.






TipA university computer?



If you cannot install software on your computer, ask your instructor about Posit Cloud, which runs RStudio in a web browser.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
3. Get the starter project
An RStudio project is a folder that holds everything for one piece of work, plus a small .Rproj file. Opening the .Rproj file opens RStudio inside that folder, so file paths like data/nhis2025_adult.csv just work.

Download nhis-project.zip (about 1.3 MB).
Unzip it and move the nhis-project folder somewhere permanent, such as your Documents folder.

On Windows, right-click the zip file and choose Extract All. Do not work inside the zip file itself; it only looks like a folder.
On a Mac, double-click the zip file.

Double-click nhis-project.Rproj to open the project in RStudio.

The folder contains:



File
What it is




nhis-project.Rproj
Opens the project


data/nhis2025_adult.csv
The NHIS teaching file from N1 and N2


prepare.R
The N2 code, as a script


n3.R … n7.R
Empty scripts, one for each lesson

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
4. A tour of RStudio
RStudio has four panes:








Pane
Where
What it is for




Source
top left
Scripts: code you write and save. Open n3.R to see it.


Console
bottom left
Where code actually runs, and where results appear


Environment
top right
The objects you have created, such as dataframes


Files
bottom right
The files in your project folder



A script is just a text file of R code. Unlike a Colab notebook, the results are not saved in the file; they appear in the Console when you run the code.
Two ways to run code from a script:

Run the current line (or selected lines): Ctrl + Enter on Windows, Cmd + Enter on a Mac.
Run the whole script from top to bottom: the Source button at the top of the script, or Ctrl + Shift + S / Cmd + Shift + S.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
5. Install the packages
Packages are installed once per computer, then loaded with library() in every script. Type this into the Console (not a script, since you never need to run it again) and press Enter:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "survey", "srvyr"))

This can take several minutes. When it finishes, check that each one loads:

library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)

Messages are normal; an error that says there is no package called ... means the installation did not finish. These lessons were tested with tidyverse 2.0.0, survey 4.5, and srvyr 1.3.1. You can check yours with packageVersion("srvyr").

survey is the standard R package for analyzing complex survey data.
srvyr lets you use survey methods with the same %>%, filter(), group_by(), and summarize() you already know. You will use it from N4 on.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
6. Run the preparation script
Open prepare.R from the Files pane. It is the code you wrote in N2, as one script. Read through it: every step should look familiar. Then click Source to run it all.
It reads the teaching file, builds the analysis variables, and saves the result as data/nhis_analysis.rds.






NoteWhy .rds and not .csv?



A CSV file holds only text and numbers. An .rds file saves an R object exactly as it is, including details such as the order of the categories you set with factor() in N2. Use saveRDS() to save and readRDS() to read.


analysis now appears in the Environment pane: 24,215 observations of 12 variables.






NoteYour turn 1



In the Console, check the analysis file with dim(analysis) and count(analysis, survivor).
Expected result: 24,215 rows and 12 columns; 2,833 survivors, 21,349 non-survivors, 33 NA.








TipSolution






dim(analysis)

[1] 24215    12

count(analysis, survivor)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  survivor     n
     <dbl> <int>
1        0 21349
2        1  2833
3       NA    33

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
7. Your first script
Now write code in n3.R, where it is saved. A script should be able to run on its own from a fresh start, so it begins by loading its packages and its data.






NoteYour turn 2



In n3.R, write a script that:

loads the tidyverse,
reads data/nhis_analysis.rds with readRDS(),
calculates, for survivors only, the percent in fair or poor health in each poverty group, as you did for education in N2.

Save the script (Ctrl + S / Cmd + S), then run it with Source.
Expected result: Below 100% 57.8%; 100-199% 40.8%; 200-399% 27.5%; 400% or more 15.7%.








TipSolution






library(tidyverse)

analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")


analysis %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor)) %>%
  group_by(poverty) %>%
  summarize(people = n(), pct_fair_poor = 100 * mean(fair_poor))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  poverty      people pct_fair_poor
  <fct>         <int>         <dbl>
1 Below 100%      206          57.8
2 100-199%        495          40.8
3 200-399%        891          27.5
4 400% or more   1239          15.7

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
8. The fresh-start test
A script that works only because of something you typed earlier in the Console will fail for anyone else, including you next week. Test it the way a stranger would run it:

Session > Restart R. This clears everything from memory; the Environment pane empties.
Run n3.R with Source.

If it still gives the same result, the script is complete. If you get an error such as object 'analysis' not found, something the script needs is missing from it.






NoteYour turn 3



Do the fresh-start test on n3.R.
Expected result: the same four percentages as before, with no errors.








TipSolution





If it failed, the most likely cause is a missing library(tidyverse) or readRDS() line at the top of the script. Every lesson script from now on starts with those two lines (plus library(srvyr) from N4).

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
In this lesson you will learn to:
Before this lesson: N3: Moving to RStudio. Work in n4.R in your starter project.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
1. Setup
Start n4.R with these lines. Every lesson script from now on starts the same way.

library(tidyverse)
library(srvyr)

analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")

If readRDS() says the file does not exist, run prepare.R first (N3, section 6).

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
2. What a weight is
Each adult in the file has a weight, WTFA_A: the number of U.S. adults that person stands for.

summary(analysis$WTFA_A)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   2358    5835    9020   10936   13371   45481 


The median person stands for about 9,000 adults, but weights range from about 2,400 to 45,000. Someone with a weight of 45,000 belongs to a group that was hard to reach or less likely to respond, so each person interviewed from that group has to stand for many more people. Someone with a small weight belongs to a group that was easy to reach.






NoteYour turn 1



Add up all the weights with sum(). What does the total represent?
Expected result: 264,821,349, about 265 million: the number of U.S. adults the survey represents (adults living in households, not in institutions such as nursing homes or prisons).








TipSolution






sum(analysis$WTFA_A)

[1] 264821349

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
3. Unweighted versus weighted
How many U.S. adults are 65 or older? Here is the share of the sample, and the share once each person counts as many people as their weight says. weighted.mean() does that.

analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_group)) %>%
  summarize(
    unweighted = 100 * mean(age_group == "65+"),
    weighted   = 100 * weighted.mean(age_group == "65+", WTFA_A)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  unweighted weighted
       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      35.06    23.26


More than a third of the people interviewed are 65 or older, but they make up less than a quarter of U.S. adults. Older adults are more likely to live alone or with just one other adult (and only one adult per household is interviewed), and they are more likely to take part, so the sample has too many of them. Each of them gets a smaller weight to make up for it.
This matters for the project because cancer is much more common at older ages. Any unweighted estimate about survivors leans toward older people.






NoteYour turn 2



What percent of U.S. adults are cancer survivors? Calculate it unweighted and weighted, leaving out people with missing survivor.
Expected result: 11.7% unweighted, 8.7% weighted.








TipSolution






analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(survivor)) %>%
  summarize(
    unweighted = 100 * mean(survivor),
    weighted   = 100 * weighted.mean(survivor, WTFA_A)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  unweighted weighted
       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      11.72    8.703

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
4. Why weights are not enough
weighted.mean() gives the right estimate. It cannot tell you how certain that estimate is, and every estimate from a sample needs a measure of uncertainty, usually a 95% confidence interval.
Uncertainty depends on how the sample was drawn, and the NHIS was not drawn one person at a time:

Clusters (sampling units). The NHIS first picks geographic areas, then households within them. People in the same area tend to be alike, so 30 people from one area tell you less than 30 people from 30 different areas. The column PPSU records each person’s primary sampling unit (PSU).
Strata. The country is first divided into groups of areas called strata, and areas are picked within each one. This makes estimates more precise. The column PSTRAT records the stratum.

Software that ignores clusters treats everyone as independent, and its confidence intervals come out too narrow: they claim more certainty than the data support.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
5. The survey design object
The srvyr package stores the data together with the design in one object. Everything after this works on that object instead of on analysis.

nhis_design <- analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(
    ids = PPSU,          # primary sampling units (clusters)
    strata = PSTRAT,     # strata
    weights = WTFA_A,    # weights
    nest = TRUE          # PSU numbers restart within each stratum
  )

nhis_design

Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement)
With (608) clusters.
Called via srvyr
Sampling variables:
  - ids: PPSU 
  - strata: PSTRAT 
  - weights: WTFA_A 
Data variables: 
  - HHX (chr), WTFA_A (dbl), PSTRAT (dbl), PPSU (dbl), fair_poor (dbl),
    survivor (dbl), poverty (fct), education (fct), age (dbl), age_group (chr),
    sex (chr), insured (chr)


Each argument names a column from the file. These four lines come straight from NCHS’s own instructions for analyzing the NHIS in R, in the 2025 survey description.






NoteWhy nest = TRUE?



PSU numbers are only unique within a stratum: two different areas in two different strata can share a number.

n_distinct(analysis$PPSU)                     # PSU numbers

[1] 606

nrow(distinct(analysis, PSTRAT, PPSU))        # actual PSUs

[1] 608


nest = TRUE tells R to identify a PSU by its stratum and its number. Without it, R would merge areas that are really separate.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
6. Estimates with confidence intervals
Use summarize() on the design object, with survey_mean() in place of mean(). vartype = "ci" asks for a 95% confidence interval, and na.rm = TRUE leaves out missing values.

nhis_design %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci"))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1    0.1472        0.1409        0.1534


survey_mean() gives a proportion. About 14.7% of U.S. adults report fair or poor health, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 14.1% to 15.3%. (The unweighted figure would have been 15.8%.)
group_by() works on the design just as it does on a dataframe.






NoteYour turn 3



Estimate the percent in fair or poor health for survivors and non-survivors, with 95% confidence intervals. Start from nhis_design, remove missing survivor with filter(), then use group_by() and survey_mean(). Multiply by 100 with mutate() if you like.
Expected result: survivors 27.4% (95% CI 25.3% to 29.5%); non-survivors 13.5% (12.9% to 14.1%).








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  filter(!is.na(survivor)) %>%
  group_by(survivor) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  survivor fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
     <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1        0     13.50         12.87         14.14
2        1     27.42         25.34         29.51


across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x) multiplies every column whose name starts with fair_poor (the estimate and both limits) by 100.



Among survivors, the weighted estimate (27.4%) is close to the unweighted one from N2 (26.9%). Weighting does not always change an estimate much, as here, but sometimes it does, as with age. You only know by doing it.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
7. Seeing what the design does
Here is the same estimate, fair or poor health among survivors, calculated three ways.

# 1. Ignoring the design: a simple confidence interval for a proportion
surv <- analysis %>% filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor))
p <- mean(surv$fair_poor)
se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nrow(surv))
c(estimate = p, low = p - 1.96 * se, high = p + 1.96 * se) * 100

estimate      low     high 
26.88096 25.24782 28.51410 

# 2. Weights only
analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(weights = WTFA_A) %>%
  filter(survivor == 1) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci") * 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1     27.42         25.45         29.39

# 3. The full design
nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci") * 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1     27.42         25.34         29.51





Method
Estimate
95% CI
Width




Ignoring the design
26.9%
25.2 to 28.5
3.3


Weights only
27.4%
25.5 to 29.4
3.9


Full design
27.4%
25.3 to 29.5
4.2




The weights fix the estimate (26.9% becomes 27.4%).
The strata and PSUs fix the uncertainty: the honest interval is about a quarter wider than the naive one.

The difference here is modest. For smaller groups and for variables that cluster strongly by place, such as income, it can be much larger. Since you cannot know in advance, always use the full design.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
8. From percentages to people
Weights also turn counts of people in the sample into counts of people in the country. survey_total() adds up the weights.






NoteYour turn 4



How many U.S. adults are cancer survivors? Use group_by(survivor) and survey_total(vartype = "ci") on nhis_design. Dividing by 1e6 (one million) makes the numbers easier to read.
Expected result: about 23.0 million survivors (95% CI 21.8 to 24.2 million). The other rows are non-survivors and people with missing survivor.








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  group_by(survivor) %>%
  summarize(adults = survey_total(vartype = "ci")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("adults"), ~ .x / 1e6))   # in millions

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  survivor   adults adults_low adults_upp
     <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1        0 241.5      233.8      249.2   
2        1  23.02      21.83      24.22  
3       NA   0.2731     0.1688     0.3774


2,833 people in the sample stand for about 23 million U.S. adults. (Remember the definition from N2: non-melanoma skin cancer alone does not count.)

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
Recap







Code
What it does




weighted.mean(x, w)
Weighted mean or proportion, without uncertainty


as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE)
The NHIS design object


survey_mean(x, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci")
Weighted mean or proportion with a 95% CI


survey_total(vartype = "ci")
Estimated number of people, with a 95% CI


group_by() on the design
Estimates for each group



The rule: weights for the estimate; strata and PSUs for the uncertainty; always all three.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
Next
Continue with N5: Weighted Estimates: estimates for subgroups, why you filter the design and never the data, comparing socioeconomic groups, and plotting estimates with confidence intervals.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
In this lesson you will learn to:
Before this lesson: N5: Weighted Estimates. Work in n6.R in your starter project.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
1. Setup
This lesson uses functions from the survey package directly, and broom (installed with the tidyverse) to tidy model results.

library(tidyverse)
library(srvyr)
library(survey)
library(broom)


analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")


nhis_design <- analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE)

survivors <- nhis_design %>% filter(survivor == 1)

survivors is the design filtered to cancer survivors (the right way, from N5). Everything in this lesson uses it.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
section: 2. Testing an association: the design-based chi-square test
text:
2. Testing an association: the design-based chi-square test
In N5 you saw that fair or poor health is much more common among survivors with lower incomes. Could a difference that large arise by chance in a sample this size? A chi-square test answers that for two categorical variables.
The ordinary chisq.test() assumes a simple random sample. svychisq() from the survey package uses the Rao-Scott correction, which accounts for weights, strata, and PSUs. It takes a formula naming the two variables, and the design.

svychisq(~ fair_poor + poverty, design = survivors)


    Pearson's X^2: Rao & Scott adjustment

data:  NextMethod()
F = 50.493, ndf = 2.9877, ddf = 1640.2560, p-value < 2.2e-16


How to read it:

F is the test statistic. Larger means stronger evidence of an association.
p-value: the probability of an association at least this strong if there really were none in the population. < 2.2e-16 is R’s way of saying “smaller than the smallest number it shows”, so report it as p < 0.001.

There is very strong evidence that self-rated health is associated with income among U.S. adult cancer survivors.






NoteYour turn 1



Test whether fair or poor health is associated with education among survivors, and then with sex. What do you conclude for each?
Expected result: education F = 58.1, p < 0.001 (strong evidence of an association); sex F = 0.47, p = 0.49 (no evidence of an association).








TipSolution






svychisq(~ fair_poor + education, design = survivors)


    Pearson's X^2: Rao & Scott adjustment

data:  NextMethod()
F = 58.11, ndf = 1.9806, ddf = 1087.3240, p-value < 2.2e-16

svychisq(~ fair_poor + sex, design = survivors)


    Pearson's X^2: Rao & Scott adjustment

data:  NextMethod()
F = 0.47132, ndf = 1, ddf = 549, p-value = 0.4927


A large p-value does not prove that men and women have the same rate. It means this sample gives no evidence of a difference.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
3. Why regression?
Income and education go together: people with more education tend to have higher incomes. So is the income gradient really about income, or partly about education? Regression estimates the association of each variable with the outcome while holding the others constant. This is called adjusting for them.
The outcome, fair_poor, is 0 or 1, so the model is logistic regression. Its results are odds ratios.

Odds and odds ratios
If 25% of a group report fair or poor health, their odds are 25 to 75, or 0.33. An odds ratio (OR) compares the odds in two groups:

OR = 1: same odds
OR = 2: twice the odds
OR = 0.5: half the odds

Every OR compares a group with a reference group. By default, R uses the first category of a factor. For poverty, that is “Below 100%”, which would give odds ratios below 1 for the other groups. Results are usually easier to read when the reference is the most advantaged group, so that every OR describes how much higher the odds are in a less advantaged group. fct_relevel() moves a category to the front.

survivors <- survivors %>%
  mutate(
    poverty = fct_relevel(poverty, "400% or more"),
    education = fct_relevel(education, "Bachelor or higher")
  )

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
4. A first model: income alone
svyglm() fits regression models on a survey design. It looks like glm(), with two differences: the data go in design =, and the family is quasibinomial(). (binomial() gives the same estimates but prints warnings about non-whole-number weights; quasibinomial() avoids them.)

model_crude <- svyglm(fair_poor ~ poverty, design = survivors, family = quasibinomial())

tidy(model_crude, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term              estimate conf.low conf.high   p.value
  <chr>                <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.2028   0.1695    0.2427 1.547e-54
2 povertyBelow 100%   6.698    4.555     9.849  1.347e-20
3 poverty100-199%     3.824    2.882     5.076  3.125e-19
4 poverty200-399%     1.865    1.433     2.427  4.206e- 6


tidy() from broom turns the model into a table. exponentiate = TRUE converts the model’s coefficients into odds ratios, and conf.int = TRUE adds 95% confidence intervals (conf.low, conf.high). select() keeps just the columns you need to read.
Read the estimate column. Compared with survivors whose family income is at least four times the poverty line, the odds of fair or poor health are about 1.9 times as high at 200-399%, 3.8 times as high at 100-199%, and 6.7 times as high below the poverty line. (Ignore the intercept row; it is the odds in the reference group, not a comparison.)
This is a crude (unadjusted) model: income alone.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
5. Adjusting for other variables
Add education, age group, and sex to the formula with +.






NoteYour turn 2



Fit model_adjusted: fair_poor explained by poverty, education, age_group, and sex. Show its odds ratios with tidy(). How does the odds ratio for “Below 100%” change compared with the crude model?
Expected result: the odds ratio for income below the poverty line falls from 6.7 (95% CI 4.6 to 9.8) to 4.7 (3.1 to 7.2). It is smaller, but still large.








TipSolution






model_adjusted <- svyglm(fair_poor ~ poverty + education + age_group + sex,
                         design = survivors, family = quasibinomial())

tidy(model_adjusted, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 9 × 5
  term                         estimate conf.low conf.high   p.value
  <chr>                           <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)                    0.1181  0.07101    0.1963 1.160e-15
2 povertyBelow 100%              4.717   3.098      7.181  1.461e-12
3 poverty100-199%                2.959   2.170      4.035  1.786e-11
4 poverty200-399%                1.545   1.171      2.039  2.153e- 3
5 educationHigh school or less   2.533   1.912      3.355  1.946e-10
6 educationSome college          1.757   1.341      2.304  4.914e- 5
7 age_group45-64                 1.118   0.6721     1.860  6.670e- 1
8 age_group65+                   1.056   0.6435     1.733  8.287e- 1
9 sexMale                        1.212   0.9740     1.508  8.466e- 2





How to read the adjusted model:

Income: among survivors with the same education, age group, and sex, those below the poverty line have about 4.7 times the odds of fair or poor health of those at 400% or more. Part of the crude association was education; most of it remains.
Education: with income held constant, survivors with a high school education or less have about 2.5 times the odds of those with a bachelor’s degree. Income and education each matter.
Age group and sex: the confidence intervals include 1, so there is no clear evidence that either is associated with fair or poor health once income and education are accounted for.

The model used 2818 survivors: people with a missing value in any variable in the formula are left out automatically.






WarningOdds ratios are not risk ratios



An odds ratio of 4.7 does not mean “4.7 times as likely”. When an outcome is common (here more than one survivor in four), odds ratios are noticeably larger than ratios of percentages. In N5, the percentages were 57.6% and 16.9%, a ratio of about 3.4. Say “odds”, not “likelihood” or “risk”, when you report odds ratios.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
6. Testing a whole variable
Poverty has three odds ratios. To ask one question, “is income associated with the outcome, after adjustment?”, test all three together with regTermTest():

regTermTest(model_adjusted, ~ poverty)

Wald test for poverty
 in svyglm(formula = fair_poor ~ poverty + education + age_group + 
    sex, design = survivors, family = quasibinomial())
F =  25.55712  on  3  and  541  df: p= 1.7848e-15 


p < 0.001: strong evidence that income is associated with fair or poor health among survivors, independent of education, age, and sex.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
section: 7. What happens if you ignore the design?
text:
7. What happens if you ignore the design?
Here is the same adjusted model fitted with ordinary glm(): no weights, no strata, no PSUs.

unweighted_model <- glm(
  fair_poor ~ poverty + education + age_group + sex,
  data = analysis %>%
    filter(survivor == 1) %>%
    mutate(
      poverty = fct_relevel(poverty, "400% or more"),
      education = fct_relevel(education, "Bachelor or higher")
    ),
  family = binomial()
)

tidy(unweighted_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term == "sexMale") %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  term    estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 sexMale    1.299    1.084     1.555 0.004510








NoteYour turn 3



Compare the sexMale row of unweighted_model with the same row of model_adjusted. Would the two models lead you to the same conclusion about sex?
Expected result: no. The unweighted model gives OR 1.30 with p = 0.005, which looks like clear evidence that men have higher odds. The design-based model gives OR 1.21 with p = 0.085 and a confidence interval that includes 1: no clear evidence.








TipSolution






tidy(model_adjusted, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term == "sexMale") %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  term    estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 sexMale    1.212   0.9740     1.508 0.08466


Ignoring the design changed both the estimate (the weights) and the uncertainty (the strata and PSUs), and together they turned “no clear evidence” into a “significant” finding. A paper built on the unweighted model would report a sex difference that the data do not support.

title: N6 · Tests and Regression
text:
8. Reporting results
A typical results sentence:

Among U.S. adult cancer survivors, fair or poor self-rated health was strongly associated with family income. After adjustment for education, age, and sex, survivors with family income below the federal poverty line had 4.7 times the odds of fair or poor health of those with income at or above 400% of the poverty line (OR 4.72, 95% CI 3.10 to 7.18).

And in the methods: the survey-weighted logistic regression, the software (R with the survey and srvyr packages), and that variance was estimated using the NHIS strata and PSUs. Lesson N7 puts this together.

text:
Recap







Code
What it does




svychisq(~ a + b, design = d)
Chi-square test with the Rao-Scott design correction


fct_relevel(x, "level")
Make “level” the reference category


svyglm(y ~ x1 + x2, design = d, family = quasibinomial())
Survey-weighted logistic regression


tidy(model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals


regTermTest(model, ~ x)
Test all categories of one variable together
